This is the second time I've had this kind of issue with Fly, where my service just goes down, Fly reports everything healthy, and there's literally no information and nothing I can really do other than wait and hope it comes back up sometime.

We had four machines (app + Postgres for staging and production) running yesterday, and three of the four (including both databases) are still down and can't be accessed... This is our company's external API app and so the issue broke all of our integrations.
As an aside, it's kind of a kick in the teeth to see the status page for our organization reporting no incidents - the same page that lists our apps as under maintenance and inaccessible!
Don't get me started with Fly — especially postgres machines. In my experience, a really nice idea with poor support and unreliable infrastructure.

We tried to migrate all our staging environments to Fly last year but it was the flakiest experience I've experienced on any PaaS. Pushing simple containers up would fail 70-80% of the time with no useful error messages and non existent support.
The worst thing about Fly is, when something goes wrong, it's not just one thing, there's bunch of things broken at the same time and their status page will show everything green.

I really want to love Fly.io... but to be honest I don't think anyone should be building mission critical applications on their service. I ended up migrating everything over to AWS because: Frequent machines not working, random outages, builds not working; Support wasn't responsive.
They had my account on some sort of shadow ban with no communication whatsoever after asking them to delete my account from their systems. I emailed them and to date never even got a response.

Fly response: 'We had a single host in the syd region go down, hard, with multiple issues... Ultimately it required a significant amount of manual work to recover... We strongly recommend running multiple instances to mitigate the impact of single-host failures like this.'
Incredibly unimpressed at fly.io staff for hiding/making private the downtime forum support thread.
We've been using fly.io for a month now. They are amazing. The service is great, the team is great, and most importantly our apps have seen a dramatic performance uplift by leveraging fly.
Had a look at the network pricing. I wouldn't host anything there. Takes 'the cloud is expensive' to a whole other level.

About Fly but not about the GPU announcement, I wish they had a S3 replacement, they suggest a GNU Affero project that is a dealbreaker for any business, needing to leave Fly to store user assets was a dealbreaker for us.

Does it have basic functioning other stuff? I am shocked at how our production usage of Fly has gone. Even basic stuff as support not being able to just... look up internal platform issues. Cryptic/non-existent error messages.
I was an early adopter of Fly.io. It is not production-ready. They should fix their basic features before adding new ones.
I use Fly.io free tier to run uptime monitoring with Uptime kuma. It works insanely well, and I'm a really happy camper.

Every time I've tried Fly... there's always a rough edge or the service breaks for me. First time I tried it, the web panel wasn't even loading. Second time, months later, everything was 500ing and I couldn't find a way to SFTP into a disk (!!!). Total dealbreaker.

My experience with Fly.io has not been a good one... Following their guide you get postgres not spinning up and linking to your app correctly and you have to nuke your entire app. The billing UI is weird and feels cobbled together.

Fly has a nice DX but unfortunately the platform still has major issues with reliability and networking. There are often problems with deploys leading to stuck and unreachable instances or other networking issues.

For me the missing bit in Fly is scheduled tasks. I know how to solve this by spinning up an app that runs permanently as a scheduler, but basic cron-like scheduling should be part of the platform IMO.

Three of four machines, including both Postgres DBs, stayed down and inaccessible. Their external API broke all integrations. The team spent a couple of hours spinning up a new Fly project to recover. They found no way to get data off the DB machines.

The org status page reported no incidents while the same page listed their apps as under maintenance and inaccessible. Another user said a dev environment was down 17 hours with no status update or notifications. Their only alert came from a third-party monitor (betterstack).

Migrated company infrastructure to AWS. Reasons: frequent machine failures, random outages, and broken builds. Support was unresponsive and kept re-asking questions despite a paid higher support tier. No sidecars, hard external monitoring integration, thin docs beyond the happy path. Still hosts hobby projects there and calls it fine for those.

Tried migrating staging environments to Fly: 'the flakiest experience I've experienced on any PaaS'. Pushing simple containers failed 70-80% of the time with no useful error messages and non-existent support.

When something breaks, many things break at once and the status page stays green. Responses are silence or casual ('this is what happens we deploy on friday'). 'A nice package around the most unreliable hosting service I've ever used.'
User asked Fly to delete their account and got no email response. Their account was put in a kind of shadow ban. They moved everything to Railway and Google Cloud Run.
Fly has a nice UX and accessible prices but is 'unstable at best'. The user is looking for alternatives for small/bootstrapped projects.
Uses Fly for side projects and has grown to like it. Considers the downtime somewhat expected and Fly's eventual explanation reasonable. Was bothered that the forum thread was made private.
Used fly.io for a month: 'They are amazing.' The service and team are great, and their apps saw a dramatic performance uplift. The poster is another YC founder who discloses the connection.
After looking at network pricing: 'I wouldn't host anything there. Takes "the cloud is expensive" to a whole other level.'
Loves Fly's simplicity, value for money and built-in VPN. The lack of an S3 replacement, with Fly suggesting an AGPL project, was a dealbreaker for their next project.

'Shocked' at how production usage went. Support couldn't look up internal platform issues, and error messages were cryptic or non-existent. 'I thought I was over Kubernetes, but Fly makes me miss it.'
Runs Uptime Kuma monitoring on the Fly.io free tier. 'It works insanely well, and I'm a really happy camper.'
On Fly GPU pricing: 'Almost twice as cheap as Modal! Very nice!'

First try: the web panel wouldn't load. Months later: everything was returning 500s and there was no way to SFTP into a disk, a dealbreaker. The same task on Render was easy (deploy from GitHub, live in minutes). Still likes Fly's mission and Elixir support.
Following Fly's guide, Postgres didn't spin up or link to the app correctly and they had to nuke the whole app. The billing UI felt cobbled together. They moved to Render, which has great dev UX.
Runs wikinewsfeed.org on Fly: very satisfied and would deploy there again. Favorite feature is automatic Prometheus metrics collection. Dislikes being charged for free Let's Encrypt certs.
Missing scheduled tasks: you have to run a permanent scheduler app. Basic cron should be part of the platform.
Dislikes usage-based pricing. On Heroku they paid $7/month and knew it would never be more, which they prefer for a fire-and-forget blog.
Migrated a small Rails project (16k monthly users) from Heroku to Helm/Kubernetes after trying Fly.io and others. Preferred the zero-downtime deploys and non-beta infrastructure, at comparable cost.
